questions.q: A company has {n} million shares priced at {p} each. What's its market cap, in £ millions?
questions.why: Market cap = shares × price: {n} million × {p} = £{answer} million.

questions.q: When you buy shares in a listed company through a platform, the company usually receives your money.
questions.why: Most trading is on the secondary market, between investors. The company only gets money when it issues new shares, such as in an IPO.

options: When a private company first sells shares to the public and lists on an exchange
When a company pays its yearly dividend
When a share price falls 10% in a day
questions.why: An Initial Public Offering is when a company floats: it raises money by selling shares and becomes listed.

questions.q: A company reports profits up 10%, but its share price falls. What's the most likely reason?
options: Investors expected more, so the result was a disappointment
Share prices always fall after results
questions.why: Prices already reflect expectations. They move on the gap between what happened and what was expected.

options: An index of the 100 largest companies on the London Stock Exchange's main market
A fund you can buy directly from the government
The 100 oldest companies in the UK
questions.why: It's the 100 biggest by market cap, reviewed every quarter, started in 1984 at 1,000.

questions.q: In the FTSE 100, a company with a higher share price always has a bigger effect on the index.
questions.why: The FTSE 100 is weighted by market cap (price × number of shares), not by share price alone.

questions.q: The FTSE 100 number on the news leaves out something important for investors. What?
questions.why: The headline index tracks prices only. Total return adds reinvested dividends, which can make a big difference.

questions.q: Match each index to what it covers.
pairs: Large and mid-sized companies in many developed countries
questions.why: Indices measure different slices of the market. Index funds track them (module 14).

questions.q: Put the life of a company going public in order.
items: Decides to raise money by floating
IPO: sells new shares to investors
Shares trade between investors on the exchange
questions.why: Private, then the decision to float, then the IPO (primary market), then everyday trading (secondary market).

questions.q: A friend says a £1 share is a better buy than a £50 share because it's cheaper. Explain why the share price alone doesn't tell you that.

ideas.label: What matters is the company's total value (market cap = price × number of shares)
You need to compare that value with profits and prospects to judge cheap or expensive

questions.model: The share price depends on how many shares the company has. What matters is its total value (market cap = price × number of shares) compared with its profits and prospects. A £1 share can be in a far more expensive company than a £50 share.
questions.why: Cheap or expensive depends on value versus profits, not the price per slice.

tests.answer: It depends on how many shares there are, so you need the market cap, and compare that to the profits.
You need to know the market cap.
Because the £50 share is a better company.

questions.q: Explain what makes a share price go up or down from minute to minute.

ideas.label: Changing expectations about future profits, news or interest rates

questions.model: The price is wherever buyers and sellers agree to trade. When more want to buy than sell, it rises; when more want to sell, it falls. What drives them is changing expectations about the company's future profits, from news, results, interest rates and the economy.
questions.why: Supply and demand, driven by expectations.

tests.answer: Supply and demand from buyers and sellers, which changes as news changes what people expect about future profits.
More buyers than sellers pushes it up.
The company sets the price each morning.
